title: Efficient Agentic GPU Kernel Optimization with a Compact Domain-Specific Language and Speed-of-Light Guidance
claim: A compact DSL program is compiled through parsing, validation, and code emission stages into a final deployable kernel wrapper.
layout: Boxes in 2 rows, left-to-right then looping back; dashed optional branch
description: A flowchart of rounded, pastel-colored boxes connected by arrows showing the compilation pipeline. The top row runs left to right. A blue input box shows kernel.dsl GEMM code with chained .with_* calls. A green 'Parse and Lower' box (Lark grammar to configuration IR) leads to a green 'Static Validation' box. These feed a large pink 'Emit Code + Wrapper' box containing a C++ namespace snippet. A dashed arrow labeled 'optional' drops from validation to a lower purple row. That row has three boxes: 'Emit CUTLASS Python API' (kernel.py), 'cutlass_cppgen', and 'Generated kernel.cu'. Labeled arrows ('send', 'emit') link them, and a dashed 'emit + wrap' arrow returns to the pink box. The boxes hold monospace code. The eye goes first to the blue input box at the top left.
caption: µCUTLASS compilation pipeline. The compiler parses and lowers a kernel.dsl program to a typed configuration IR, validates architecture and other constraints, and emits the CUTLASS C++ code in a wrapper header (ucutlass hash.h). Optionally, it emits a CUTLASS Python API plan (kernel.py) and invokes cutlass cppgen to produce kernel.cu, which is then wrapped into the final header.
abstract: LLM agents can optimize GPU kernels, but each candidate requires generation, compilation, correctness testing, and profiling. Our objective is to reduce the number of expensive attempts needed to find a correct, fast kernel. We study two complementary ways to improve this attempt efficiency by changing the representation that the agent writes in and adding a first-principles performance signal that estimates remaining headroom. We introduce $\mu$CUTLASS, a compact in-context learnable DSL that exposes high-impact CUTLASS optimization choices while hiding template plumbing, and pair it with Speed-of-Light (SOL) guidance for search steering, budget allocation, and integrity checking. On 59 KernelBench problems on H100, switching GPT-5-mini from low-level code generation to $\mu$CUTLASS changes a $0.40\times$ geomean regression versus PyTorch into a $1.27\times$ speedup. Adding SOL-guided steering, it reaches $1.56\times$. Across model tiers, this combination lets weaker models match or exceed stronger raw-code baselines, and SOL-guided scheduling saves 19--43\% of tokens while retaining at least 95\% geomean speedup. We also show that integrity filtering is essential because, without SOL-assisted checks, reported speedups can be inflated by up to $1.9\times$ by benchmark-gaming or PyTorch-only solutions.
